IRAC_summ:
Case Name: CITGO Petro. Corp. v. Ascot Underwriting Ltd., 2025 U.S. App. LEXIS 28170.
Court: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit.
Area of Law: Insurance Law—Marine Cargo; Contract Interpretation.
Procedural Posture: Appeal from a judgment awarding damages to the insured following summary judgment and a jury trial.
Issue
The defendant reinsurers appeal a judgment awarding over $54 million to CITGO for the loss of crude oil seized by the Maduro regime in Venezuela. The core legal dispute concerns the interpretation of the term "insurrection" in a marine cargo insurance policy. Specifically, the court must determine whether the district court erred in granting summary judgment by finding the term ambiguous and concluding, as a matter of law, that the actions of the Maduro regime—retaining power through violence against the recognized interim government of Juan Guaidó—constituted an "insurrection." This involves applying the "recognition doctrine" to determine the "constituted government" against which the insurrection was directed. Additionally, the court must decide whether the district court abused its discretion in taking judicial notice of political facts from government reports and whether the jury instruction on "but-for" causation was proper under New York law given the policy language "arising from," or if the defendants waived their objection to that instruction.
Rule
Under New York law, ambiguous insurance terms are construed against the insurer (contra proferentem). "Insurrection" is defined as a violent uprising by a group acting for the specific purpose of overthrowing the constituted government and seizing its powers (Pan Am.). The "recognition doctrine" binds federal courts to the Executive Branch's recognition of foreign governments (Zivotofsky). Judicial notice may be taken of facts not subject to reasonable dispute from reliable sources (Fed. R. Evid. 201). In insurance contracts, the phrase "arising from" or "arising out of" generally triggers a "but-for" causation standard, whereas "proximately caused by" is narrower (Burlington Ins. Co.). Objections to jury instructions are waived if explicitly withdrawn at trial (Spruill).
Application
The court affirmed the summary judgment ruling that an "insurrection" occurred. It agreed that the term was ambiguous in the policy and properly applied the Pan Am. definition [*26]. The court held that the "constituted government" element was satisfied by the U.S. Executive's recognition of Juan Guaidó as the legitimate president; the court was bound by this determination under the recognition doctrine [*35]. Consequently, the Maduro regime's violent refusal to cede power and its attacks on the Guaidó government constituted an "uprising" with the intent to overthrow the constituted authority [*31]. The court rejected the argument that an insurrection requires the insurgents to lack de facto control, noting that the unique situation of a regime retaining power against a recognized government fit the broad construction required by contra proferentem [*32].
Regarding judicial notice, the court found no abuse of discretion. The district court properly noticed the fact of Guaidó's recognition and other undisputed political events from reliable government sources like the State Department, while carefully excluding disputed opinions [*43].
Finally, on the jury instruction issue, the court held that the reinsurers waived their objection to the "but-for" causation standard by explicitly withdrawing it at trial [*50]. Even on the merits, the court found that the policy language "arising from" supports a "but-for" standard under New York law (Maroney), distinguishing it from the "proximate cause" standard often applied in marine insurance when different language is used [*52].
Conclusion
The judgment of the district court is affirmed.

case_name: Crown Prosecution Service v Aquila Advisory Ltd [2021] UKSC 49
case:
Crown Prosecution Service v Aquila Advisory Ltd [2021] All ER (D) 15 (Nov)
Page 1 of 4
Crown Prosecution Service v Aquila Advisory Ltd [2021] All ER (D) 15 (Nov)
[2021] UKSC 49
Supreme Court
Lord Lloyd-Jones, Lord Sales, Lord Burrows, Lord Stephens and Lady Rose SCJJ
3 November 2021
COMPANY – FRAUDULENT TRADING – CONFISCATION ORDER
Abstract
The Supreme Court (the court), in dismissing the Crown Prosecution Service's appeal, held that the Court of 
Appeal, Civil Division, had not erred in holding that, for the purposes of a proprietary claim by a company against its 
directors to recover proceeds of crime received in breach of fiduciary duty, the illegality of the directors was not 
attributed to the company, notwithstanding that the company itself had suffered no loss and stood to profit from the 
illegal acts. In earlier proceedings, confiscation orders had been made against two individuals who had exploited 
their position as directors of a company (VTL) in breach of their fiduciary duty, to make a secret profit of £4.55m. 
Subsequently, a declaration had been made that £4.55m was held on constructive trust in favour of VTL, whose 
rights had since been assigned to the respondent company. The court held that Bilta (UK) Ltd (in liquidation) and 
others v Nazir [2015] 2 All ER 1083 (which was authority for the proposition that the unlawful acts or dishonest state 
of mind of a director could not be attributed to the company, so as to afford the director an illegality defence to the 
company's claim against him for breach of fiduciary duty) remained good law, and that it applied to the present 
case. The court rejected the contention that the Court of Appeal's decision was inconsistent with the regime 
established by the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002, and it ruled that, even if there had been a discretion to grant 
declaratory relief, it had appropriately been exercised.
Digest
The judgment is available at: [2021] UKSC 49
  Background     
F and P (the directors) exploited their position as directors of a company (VTL), in breach of their fiduciary duty, to 
make a secret profit of £4.55m. The amount of £4.55m was also the benefit obtained by the directors from their 
crime of cheating the public revenue by dishonestly facilitating and inducing others to submit false claims for tax 
relief. VTL went into administration. The respondent company (Aquila) was assigned VTL's proprietary rights. 
Following the directors' criminal convictions, the appellant Crown Prosecution Service (the CPS) sought 
confiscation orders against them, under the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 (POCA 2002). Subsequently, P was 
ordered to pay £809,692, and F was ordered to pay £648,000. 
Aquila contended that the directors should be treated as having acquired the benefit of the secret profit on behalf of 
VTL and that, as a result, the £4.55m was beneficially owned by VTL under a constructive trust, and that the 
beneficial interest in that trust had been assigned to Aquila. 
*Crown Prosecution Service v Aquila Advisory Ltd [2021] All ER (D) 15 (Nov)
Page 2 of 4
Accordingly, Aquila argued that because it had a proprietary claim to the secret profit of £4.55m, its claim took 
priority over the confiscation orders, which did not give the CPS any form of proprietary interest. If that was correct, 
Aquila would be entitled to all of the directors' assets, leaving nothing to satisfy the confiscation orders. 
The  judge (the judge) granted a declaration that an amount of £4.55m was held on constructive trust in favour of 
VTL, whose rights had since been assigned to Aquila. Further, and in accordance with an agreement between the 
parties, the trial judge declared that the CPS was obliged to give instructions for the transfer of the net proceeds 
realised from all the assets listed in the confiscation orders to Aquila. 
The CPS appealed to the Court of Appeal, Civil Division, contending that the directors' actions should have been 
attributed to VTL and,  therefore, that VTL should have been barred from recovering any proceeds of crime 
because of the principle of illegality, namely that a person should not be permitted to benefit from his or her illegal 
act. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. 
The CPS appealed to the Supreme Court.
  Issues and decisions     
(1) Whether, as the CPS contended, the Court of Appeal had erred in concluding that the facts of the present case 
fell within the ratio of Bilta (UK) Ltd (in liquidation) and others v Nazir [2015] 2 All ER 1083, and whether it had erred 
in holding that, for the purposes of a proprietary claim by a company against its directors to recover proceeds of 
crime received in breach of fiduciary duty, the illegality of the directors was not attributed to the company, 
notwithstanding that the company itself had suffered no loss and stood to profit from the illegal acts.
The reasoning of the present court in Bilta, albeit concerned with loss-based claims, rather than claims to strip 
profits, applied with equal force to the breach of fiduciary duty which was the subject of the present decision. Bilta 
was authority for the proposition that the unlawful acts or dishonest state of mind of a director could not be 
attributed to the company, so as to afford the director an illegality defence to the company's claim against him for 
breach of fiduciary duty. The principles of illegality in Patel v Mirza [2017] 1 All ER 191 simply did not arise.  
Although the law on illegality had been restated since Bilta by the present court in Patel, its reasoning, built as it 
was on the policy of avoiding illegality undermining the purpose of the rule in question, was entirely consistent with 
Patel, and had not been undermined by it. Accordingly, Bilta remained good law after Patel (see [61], [81] of the 
judgment).
It was clear, since the decision in FHR European Ventures LLP v Mankarious [2014] 4 All ER 79 that, as between 
the principal and his agent, any benefit obtained by the agent in breach of his fiduciary duty was held on trust for his 
principal, regardless of the circumstances in which it had been obtained. Although, as far as secret profits were 
concerned, that might be said already to have been clear law prior to FHR, the present court agreed with the Court 
of Appeal (at paragraph 19) that: 'The decision in FHR therefore prevents a director in the position of [F] and [P] 
from asserting a right to retain the secret profit against VTL based on the fact that it has been obtained by fraud' 
(see [50] of the judgment). 
In civil proceedings brought by a company against its directors for breach of fiduciary duty, claiming that the sums 
they acquired as a result of the breach had been subject to a constructive trust in the company's favour, the 
principles established in Bilta prevented the attribution of the dishonesty of those directors to that company. In that 
way, the rules of attribution prevented the directors' dishonesty from being attributed to the company, with the result 
that the company was not acting illegally and its claim was not barred by the defence of illegality. Attribution being 
denied, the illegality defence failed (see [59] of the judgment).
The CPS asserted that the purpose of the rule as to attribution was not to protect a company when a feature of a 
fraudulent scheme was that the company stood to profit from it, and that attribution should only be denied where the 
dishonest conduct was targeted against the company, so that it was intended to, or did, in fact, sustain a financial 
loss, but not where the dishonest conduct was intended to, or did, in fact, secure a financial benefit for the company 
(see [70] of the judgment).
*Crown Prosecution Service v Aquila Advisory Ltd [2021] All ER (D) 15 (Nov)
Page 3 of 4
That argument was misconceived. The relevant rule was the duty owed by an officer to the company which the 
officer served. The purpose of the rule, itself, meant that the company could not be identified with its officers. That 
meant that the wrongful acts of the directors in breach of their director's duties could not be attributed to the 
company. It could make no difference to the reasoning in Bilta whether the claim brought by the company against 
its directors was for loss suffered by the company or for gains made by the directors or if a part of the director's 
scheme was that, not only the director would benefit, but so also would the company. The director's duty to the 
company would still be negated if there was an exception to the reasoning in Bilta that attributed a director's 
wrongdoing to the company in circumstances where the director's scheme in breach of his fiduciary duty to the 
company also included an element of actual or intended profit for the company (see [71] of the judgment).
The CPS's argument was also rejected on the fundamental basis that the constructive trust existed to ensure 
compliance with, and was imposed in consequence of, the directors' fiduciary duty to the company. It would 
fundamentally undermine that fiduciary duty if the director could establish that a constructive trust did not arise 
purely on the basis that the director also intended that the company should make a financial profit, or on the basis 
that in fact the company had made a financial profit, so that the director should be able to retain the director's own 
unlawful profit. Such a consequence could not be correct (see [74] of the judgment). 
Another reason for rejecting the CPS's argument was that it undermined the prophylactic way in which the director's 
fiduciary duties operated (see [75] of the judgment).
Further, and among other things, it was immaterial whether the dishonesty relied on related to the same acts as 
formed the 'very matter' of the claim or related to collateral acts of dishonesty. In either case, reliance was still being 
placed on the wrongdoing of the same directors who were defendants to the company's claim to defeat that claim 
by attributing their own dishonesty to the company. Attribution would not be permitted in those circumstances 
regardless as to how the dishonesty of the directors was formulated and regardless as to whether the dishonesty 
was the 'very matter' complained of, or whether it was another aspect of that matter (see [77]-[80] of the judgment).
Bilta (UK) Ltd (in liquidation) and others v Nazir [2015] UKSC 23, [2015] 2 All ER 1083, [2015] 2 WLR 1168, [2015] 
All ER (D) 149 (Apr) applied
FHR European Ventures LLP v Mankarious [2014] UKSC 45, [2014] 4 All ER 79, [2014] 3 WLR 535, [2014] All ER 
(D) 156 (Jul) applied
Patel v Mirza [2016] UKSC 42, [2017] 1 All ER 191, [2016] 3 WLR 399, [2016] All ER (D) 91 (Jul) considered
Singularis Holdings Ltd (in liquidation) v Daiwa Capital Markets Europe Ltd [2019] UKSC 50, [2020] 1 All ER 383, 
[2019] 3 WLR 997, [2019] All ER (D) 182 (Oct) considered
(2) Whether the Court of Appeal's decision was inconsistent with the regime established by POCA 2002. 
The CPS submitted that POCA 2002 was intended to permit innocent third-party purchasers, who had paid market 
value for criminal property, to keep it, and innocent third-party victims, who had suffered loss as a result of criminal 
behaviour, to be compensated, in each case in priority to the state, but not to permit third parties otherwise to 
benefit from the actions of criminals any more than those criminals themselves.
The contention that the Court of Appeal's decision was inconsistent with the regime established by POCA 2002 was 
rejected (see [87] of the judgment).
The scheme of POCA 2002 was not to interfere with any property rights (except tainted gifts). POCA 2002 
protected the property rights of others regardless as to how those rights arose. Furthermore, there were specific 
provisions in POCA 2002 which permitted the state to override property rights, but those provisions had not been 
used by the CPS. The operation of POCA 2002 had not been frustrated by the proprietary claim, as the CPS had 
had the right to seek to recover the proceeds of crime from VTL in a number of ways, but it had not sought to invoke 
those rights. It had not availed itself of remedies under POCA 2002 Pts 2 and 5. It was not permissible to use public 
*Crown Prosecution Service v Aquila Advisory Ltd [2021] All ER (D) 15 (Nov)
Page 4 of 4
policy considerations said to derive from Pt 7 to alter the existing property rights under a constructive trust (see [36]
[38], [83], [86] of the judgment).
The scheme of POCA 2002 contained in Pts 2 and 5, like the scheme of Drug Trafficking Offences Act 1986 (DTOA 
1986), was not to interfere with existing third-party property rights. Rather Pts 2 and 5 contained provisions which 
could be used to override the property rights of VTL by a confiscation order on conviction in the Crown Court or by 
civil recovery of the proceeds of unlawful conduct. Furthermore, there was provision for a restraint order to prevent 
VTL from dealing with its proprietary rights before an application for a confiscation order could be determined (see 
[84]-[86] of the judgment).
Norris, Re [2001] UKHL 34, [2001] 3 All ER 961, [2001] 1 WLR 1388, [2001] All ER (D) 319 (Jun) considered
Bowman v Fels [2005] EWCA Civ 226, [2005] 4 All ER 609, [2005] 1 WLR 3083, [2005] 2 FLR 247, [2005] All ER 
(D) 115 (Mar) considered
R (on the application of Best) v Chief Land Registrar (Secretary of State for Justice, interested party) [2015] EWCA 
Civ 17, [2015] 4 All ER 495, [2015] 3 WLR 1505, [2015] All ER (D) 153 (Jan) considered
(3) Whether the judge had erred in granting Aquila declaratory relief.
The CPS submitted that, even if the unlawful conduct of the former directors could not be attributed to VTL, then the 
judge, in the proper exercise of his discretion, ought not to have granted Aquila any declaratory relief. 
Aquila submitted that the grant of a declaration had not been subject to the exercise of discretion.
Even if there had been a discretion to grant declaratory relief, then, plainly, it had appropriately been exercised. 
Constructive trusts were not remedial, but institutional. In other words, in the present context, the constructive trust 
(and the principal's beneficial ownership of the property) had arisen automatically at the moment that, in breach of 
their fiduciary duty, the directors had received the secret profits. There had never been a moment at which the 
former directors, as fiduciaries, had owned the profits in equity. The declaration granted by the judge had not only 
had the effect of recognising that state of affairs, but it had also accorded with the terms of the settlement 
agreements entered into by the CPS (see [88] of the judgment).
Foskett v McKeown [2001] 1 AC 102, [2000] 3 All ER 97, [2000] 2 WLR 1299, [2000] All ER (D) 687 considered
FHR European Ventures LLP v Mankarious [2013] EWCA Civ 17, [2013] 3 All ER 29, [2013] 3 WLR 466, [2013] All 
ER (D) 219 (Jan) considered
Decision of Court of Appeal, Civil Division [2019] All ER (D) 59 (Apr) affirmed.
Andrew Sutcliffe QC, Julian Christopher QC and Anne Jeavons (instructed by CPS National Proceeds of Crime 
Unit) for the CPS.
Stuart Ritchie QC, Martin Evans QC and Sam Neaman (instructed by Kingsley Napley LLP) for Aquila.
 This content is based on the case summary published by the UK Supreme Court and is published with permission. 
The original summary can be found here: https://www.supremecourt.uk/press-summary/uksc-2019-0105.html.
End of Document
IRAC_summ:
Case Name: Crown Prosecution Service v Aquila Advisory Ltd [2021] UKSC 49
Court + jurisdiction: United Kingdom Supreme Court
Area of law: Company Law – Illegality – Constructive Trusts – Proceeds of Crime
Procedural posture: Appeal from the Court of Appeal, Civil Division
Issue
Whether a company can assert a proprietary claim (constructive trust) over the secret profits made by its directors through fraud and breach of fiduciary duty, in priority to a confiscation order obtained by the Crown, or whether the directors' illegality is attributed to the company to bar its claim.
Rule
Directors who acquire benefits in breach of fiduciary duty hold them on constructive trust for the company (FHR European Ventures). Under Bilta (UK) Ltd v Nazir, the unlawful acts or dishonest state of mind of directors cannot be attributed to the company in a claim by the company against those directors for breach of duty. This "breach of duty" exception to attribution applies even if the company suffered no loss or stood to profit from the fraud. The Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 (POCA) does not override existing third-party property rights (like a constructive trust) except through specific statutory mechanisms.
Application
The directors of VTL made secret profits of £4.55m through tax fraud. VTL (via its assignee, Aquila) claimed this sum was held on constructive trust. The CPS sought to enforce confiscation orders against the directors' assets, arguing VTL's claim was barred by illegality because the directors' fraud should be attributed to VTL.
The Court rejected the CPS's argument. Applying Bilta, the Court held that a company cannot be identified with its directors when it is the victim of their breach of duty. Attributing the directors' fraud to the company to defeat its claim for breach of duty would undermine the very fiduciary duties the law seeks to enforce [59], [74]. The Court dismissed the argument that Bilta only applies where the company suffers loss; the principle applies equally where the company seeks to strip illicit profits, even if the fraud was intended to benefit the company [71].
Furthermore, the Court held that recognizing VTL's proprietary interest was not inconsistent with POCA 2002. POCA is not designed to confiscate property belonging to innocent third parties (here, VTL/Aquila). Since the directors held the funds on trust for VTL from the moment of receipt, the funds were not the directors' assets available for confiscation [83]–[88].
Conclusion
The Court held that the directors' illegality was not attributed to the company, validating the company's proprietary claim over the proceeds in priority to the confiscation order; the appeal was dismissed.

case_name: Hastings v Finsbury Orthopaedics Ltd and another (Scotland) [2022] UKSC 19
case:
Hastings v Finsbury Orthopaedics Ltd and another (Scotland) [2022] All ER (D) 90 (Jun)
Hastings v Finsbury Orthopaedics Ltd and another (Scotland) [2022] All ER 
(D) 90 (Jun)
[2022] UKSC 19
Supreme Court
Lord Reed P, Lord Kitchin, Lord Stephens, Lady Rose and Lord Lloyd-Jones SCJJ
29 June 2022
CONSUMER PROTECTION – CONSUMER SAFETY – DEFECT
Abstract
The Supreme Court dismissed the appellant's appeal against the decision of the Outer House of the Court of 
Session that the MITCH–Accolade product (the product) manufactured by the respondents and used in the 
appellant's metal on metal (MoM) total hip replacement was not defective within the meaning of s 3 the Consumer 
Protection Act 1987 (which implemented Council Directive (EEC) 85/374 (the Directive)) on the basis that the 
appellant had not proved, on the balance of probabilities, that the entitled expectation in relation to the product at 
the time of its supply to him was not met or that there was a defect in the product so as to give rise to liability on the 
part of the respondents under the Act. The Inner House of the Court of Session refused the appellant's reclaiming 
motion. The appellant relied, among other things, on the conduct of the respondents in withdrawing the product 
from the market and the notices and alerts issued by regulators and by the respondents. The court held that the 
appellant had failed to establish his case on a statistical basis; the evidence and expressions of concern related to 
the performance of MoM prostheses in general. The court was entitled and required to have regard to material 
available at the time of proof which was not available at the time when the notices were issued. Accordingly, it was 
not open to the court to interfere with the judge's findings of fact. In the circumstances, there was no scope for the 
application of the principle of effectiveness in EU law, any principle of EU law which might require greater weight to 
be attached to considerations of consumer protection, or any domestic law principle of fairness which might require 
a benevolent application of the Act.
Digest
The judgment is available at: [2022] UKSC 19
  Background     
In 2009, the appellant, H, underwent a metal-on-metal (MoM) total hip replacement (THR) using the MITCH
Accolade product (the product) which was manufactured by the respondents. In 2012, the appellant underwent 
revision of the hip implant in his left hip. Subsequently, H brought proceedings claiming that the replacement hip 
used in that operation was defective and sought damages under s 2 of the Consumer Protection Act 1989 (CPA 
1987). 
At first instance, the issues in the case were limited to the question of whether the product used in H's operation 
was 'defective' within the meaning of CPA 1987 s 3. That Act implemented Council Directive (EEC) 85/374 (the 
Directive) on European product liability. H sought to prove that the product was defective by demonstrating design 
flaws. In that regard, he maintained: (i) that the metal debris created by the product had given rise to a greater risk 
of an adverse effect on the patient and so a greater risk of early failure, in comparison with debris produced by non
Page 2 of 4
*Hastings v Finsbury Orthopaedics Ltd and another (Scotland) [2022] All ER (D) 90 (Jun)
metal-on-metal (non-MoM) prostheses; (ii) that design features of the product created a greater risk of early failure 
than with non-MoM prostheses; and (iii) that the outcome after revision was worse with the product. H also relied on 
matters which were said to constitute prima facie evidence that the product was defective, in particular on 
expressions of professional concern by the orthopaedic community, the conduct of the respondents in withdrawing 
the product from the market and the notices and alerts issued by regulators and by the respondents. H maintained 
that those matters established that the product was defective for the purposes of CPA 1987. 
The Outer House of the Court of Session held after a preliminary proof that the appellant had failed on the statistical 
evidence to prove that the product was defective. The judge had identified two criteria of entitled expectation in 
relation to the product: time to revision (survivorship); and prospects of success of revision surgery (which was not 
relevant to the appeal). The judge found that the data from 2012, which informed the Medicines and Healthcare 
Products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) alert, and the latest available data from 2018 were consistent in showing, 
prima facie, a revision rate for MoM THRs significantly worse than rates for available alternatives. However, he 
observed that the thrust of the expert's report demonstrated that the use of those figures as a measure of 
survivorship would create a misleading impression for a number of reasons, namely that the data was incomplete, 
limited or biased and concluded that H had not proved, on balance of probabilities, at the time his prostheses were 
supplied, either: (i) that survivorship was worse for the product than for existing alternative products that could have 
been implanted instead; or (ii) that use of the product had given rise to an increased risk that revision surgery, in the 
event of its failure, would be unlikely to achieve as satisfactory an outcome as if the primary implant had been one 
of the existing alternatives. Therefore, H had not proved, on balance of probabilities, that the entitled expectation in 
relation to the product at the time of its supply to him was not met and it followed that he had not proved, on 
balance of probabilities, that there was a defect in the product so as to give rise to liability on the part of the 
respondents under CPA 1987. The Inner House of the Court of Session refused H's reclaiming motion. 
H appealed. 
  Issues and decisions     
Whether the judge was, after a further consideration of the evidence, entitled to reach a conclusion that, 
notwithstanding the prima facie evidence, H had failed to overcome the burden of proof.
H submitted that, notwithstanding the statistical evidence, it was open to him to prove his case by reference to 
evidence which established a prima facie case that the product did not meet the entitled expectation. That evidence 
comprised the response of the orthopaedic community, the response of the national regulator and the response of 
the respondents themselves leading to their withdrawing the product from the market. Relying on EU law, H 
submitted that: (i) the approach taken by the judge had made it excessively difficult for him to prove his case, that 
the medical research neither confirmed nor ruled out that the product was defective and requiring the appellant to 
prove his case by statistics, without recourse to the other evidence on which the appellant relied, undermined the 
effectiveness of the Directive; and (ii) the provision of the Directive had to be interpreted so far as possible in favour 
of the party to whom protection was intended to be given, namely the consumer. Further, he submitted that he had 
been set an impossible task, that of proving his case by statistics that were not available to him on account of the 
respondent's actions in withdrawing the product from the market and that the domestic principle of fairness entitled 
the court to draw an inference that the product was defective and that it should do so, as a matter of common sense 
and fairness, unless there was further evidence before the court such that it considered it inappropriate to do so.
The appeal was unusual in that the legal issues concerning the application of CPA 1987 were largely agreed. The 
relevant principles were that CPA 1987 (and the Directive which it implemented) had introduced a system of no
fault liability in respect of defective products. The test was whether the safety of the product was not such as 
persons generally were entitled to expect. What persons generally were entitled to expect would be assessed 
having regard to all the circumstances which were factually or legally relevant to the evaluation of safety, including 
the matters identified in CPA 1987 s 3(2). That had to be evaluated at the time when the product was supplied by its 
producer to another. The assessment of risks associated with a product, which might inform entitled expectations 
as to its safety, had to be done at the time the product was supplied and not with the benefit of hindsight. The 
burden of proof was on the consumer to establish a defect and a causal link to the injury (see [15] of the judgment).
Page 3 of 4
*Hastings v Finsbury Orthopaedics Ltd and another (Scotland) [2022] All ER (D) 90 (Jun)
The nature of the product was such that there could be no entitlement to an absolute level of safety. The test of 
entitled expectation was whether the level of safety of the product would not be worse, when measured by 
appropriate criteria, than existing non–MoM products that would otherwise have been used (see [19] of the 
judgment).
The judge had been entitled to hold that, when the up-to-date information had been considered, the concerns, 
alerts and warnings had lacked a sound underlying scientific or statistical base. The appellant had failed to establish 
his case on a statistical basis. The evidence and the expressions of concern related to the performance of MoM 
prostheses in general. It was not in dispute that the reported revision rates of MoM prostheses varied from product 
to product, the judge had not sought to review MoM prostheses as an entire class or to analyse the performance of 
other MoM prostheses. Given the wide range of revision rates in the case of MoM prostheses generally and the fact 
that the revision rates for MoM prostheses were typically higher than those for non-MoM prostheses, the 
generalised expressions of professional concern had not assisted the appellant in establishing that the product was 
defective (see [36], [41], [43] of the judgment).
The judge's predominant consideration was that sales of MoM THRs generally had sharply declined. The product 
was withdrawn from the market in 2011 before any Medical Device Alert was issued in relation to the product 
specifically, as opposed to MoM prostheses generally. Therefore, the judge found, and was clearly entitled to find, 
that the withdrawal of the product was brought about by commercial considerations. As a result, the circumstances 
and reasons for the withdrawal of the product from the market had not provided any support for H's case that the 
product was defective (see [45]-[47] of the judgment).
The notices and alerts issued by regulators and the respondents had not assisted the appellant. The evidence 
appeared to support a failure to meet the applicable standard of entitled expectation. However, they could not of 
themselves be determinative of the issue whether there was a breach of an entitled expectation. In assessing 
whether there had been compliance with an entitled expectation the court was entitled and required to have regard 
to material available at the time of proof, which was not available in 2012 when the notices were issued. By the time 
of proof in 2019 there was, in evidence before the Outer House, a statistical analysis by the expert which had not 
been contested by H. The prima facie evidence provided by the notices had to be examined in the light of such of 
the conclusions of the expert as were accepted by the judge. The reasoning, which had led the expert to the 
conclusion that H's case of a breach of entitled expectation was not made out on a statistical basis, applied equally 
to the category of prima facie evidence: the judge's conclusions contradicted H's case founded on statistics and, for 
the same reasons, contradicted the information then available which formed the basis of the concerns, alerts and 
safety notices in the years 2010 to 2013. The expert's evidence did not leave the category of prima facie evidence 
unchallenged; on the contrary it undermined it (see [61], [62] of the judgment).
Further, in agreement with the Lord President, the fact that the judge had expressed his conclusion in terms of the 
burden of proof had not invalidated his reasoning. The appellant had simply failed to prove the existence of a defect 
and the present appeal was no more than an attempt to appeal against the judge's findings of fact. It was not open 
to the court to interfere with those findings. In the circumstances, there was no scope for the application of the 
principle of effectiveness in EU law, any principle of EU law which might require greater weight to be attached to 
considerations of consumer protection, or any domestic law principle of fairness which might require a benevolent 
application of the CPA 1987 (see [64], [65] of the judgment).
Accordingly, the appeal would be dismissed (see [66] of the judgment).

IRAC_summ:
Case Name: Hastings v Finsbury Orthopaedics Ltd and another (Scotland) [2022] UKSC 19
Court + jurisdiction: United Kingdom Supreme Court
Area of law: Consumer Protection – Product Liability
Procedural posture: Appeal from the Inner House of the Court of Session.
Issue
Whether a consumer proved that a "metal-on-metal" hip prosthesis was "defective" under section 3 of the Consumer Protection Act 1987 based on "prima facie" evidence including regulatory alerts and the product's withdrawal from the market, where statistical evidence at trial failed to demonstrate performance worse than non-metal alternatives.
Rule
Under the Consumer Protection Act 1987 (implementing Directive 85/374/EEC), a product is defective if its safety is not such as persons generally are entitled to expect. The burden of proof lies on the consumer. The entitled expectation is assessed at the time of supply, considering all relevant circumstances, but is not an expectation of absolute safety. While subsequent events (like regulatory alerts) can be evidence of a defect, the court must assess such prima facie evidence against all material available at the time of proof, including up-to-date statistical analysis.
Application
The Court emphasized that the "entitled expectation" for the hip implant was not absolute safety, but that its level of safety would not be worse than existing non-metal-on-metal (MoM) products [19]. The claimant relied heavily on the fact that the product (MITCH-Accolade) was withdrawn from the market and that regulators had issued safety alerts regarding MoM implants.
The Court held that the trial judge was entitled to find that the withdrawal of the product was driven by commercial considerations rather than safety defects, stripping that fact of probative value [45]–[47]. Regarding the regulatory alerts, the Court reasoned that while these constituted prima facie evidence, they were not determinative. The judge was required to test this prima facie evidence against the expert statistical analysis available at the time of the trial. The expert evidence demonstrated that the generalized concerns underlying the earlier alerts lacked a sound statistical basis when applied to this specific product [61]–[62].
Because the claimant failed to prove via statistics that the product’s revision rates were materially worse than the alternatives, and because the expert evidence undermined the basis of the regulatory alerts, the claimant failed to discharge the burden of proof. The Court reiterated that it could not interfere with the trial judge’s findings of fact unless there was no evidence to support them, which was not the case here [64]–[65].
Conclusion
The Court held that the appellant failed to prove the product was defective because the statistical evidence rebutted the inference drawn from regulatory alerts and market withdrawal; the appeal was dismissed.

Commonwealth v. Appellant
Superior Court of Pennsylvania

October 28, 2025, Filed

Reporter

COMMONWEALTH OF PENNSYLVANIA v. RICHARD M. BETTIS Appellant 

Notice: Decision text below is the first available text from the court; it has not been editorially reviewed by 
LexisNexis. Publisher's editorial review, including Headnotes, Case Summary, Shepard's analysis or any 
amendments will be added in accordance with LexisNexis editorial guidelines.

Core Terms

arrest, trespass, defiant, disorderly conduct, harassment, mask, alarm, resisting arrest, trial court, annoy, school 
police, weight of the evidence, misdemeanor, appointment, school building, resistance, paperwork, public 
inconvenience, high school, post-sentence, license, inside, sufficient evidence, arrested appellant, school grounds, 
wrestle, wear, conversation, disturb, scuffle

Opinion

 [*1] Appeal from the Judgment of Sentence Entered July 22, 2024

In the Court of Common Pleas of Westmoreland County Criminal Division

at No(s): CP-65-CR-0000137-2022

BEFORE: BOWES, J., STABILE, J., and BENDER, P.J.E.

OPINION BY BENDER, P.J.E.: FILED: October 28, 2025

Richard M. Bettis (Appellant) appeals from the judgment of sentence of

one year of probation, imposed following his convictions for resisting arrest,

defiant trespass, disorderly conduct, and harassment.1 He challenges the

authority of the school police officers to arrest him, the sufficiency of the

evidence for his convictions, and also claims that the guilty verdicts are

contrary to the weight of the evidence provided. We affirm.2



Page 2 of 13
Commonwealth v. Appellant, 2025 PA Super 244

1 18 Pa.C.S. 5104, 3503(b)(1)(i), 5503(a)(1), and 2709(a)(1), respectively.

2 On August 4, 2025, the day before oral argument was scheduled in this appeal, defense counsel filed an 
application to move oral argument to the expedited list. As the motion was filed the day before arguments, the panel 
did not have the time to issue a formal order granting the request. Nonetheless, this case was argued on an 
expedited basis. We therefore deny the outstanding defense motion as moot.

Charges in this case surround Appellant's actions on September 10,

2021. The trial [*2]  court set forth the facts of this incident as follows:

Hempfield Area School District Police Officer Shannon Binda testified that, on September 10, 2021, he was 
checking people in at the high school front desk, along with Chief [Len] Lander. A female student was sitting next to 
the front desk at that time.

[Appellant] came to the front doors and was "buzzed in" by the officers. [Appellant] wanted to speak to the principal 
and deliver paperwork to make the school administration aware of the change in masking requirements, stating that 
the mask requirement was unconstitutional. [Appellant] was asked to put on a mask, but refused. [Appellant] stated 
that he had an underlying medical condition. [Appellant] conceded that the officers offered to step outside with him 
to talk about it. [Appellant] refused to leave the building. [Appellant] did not have an appointment so Officer Binda 
denied him entry to the school and offered to pass along the information he had for the principal. [Appellant] stated 
that he had a right to be there and the officers could not tell him otherwise. He said that he spoke to an attorney and 
he had a right to be inside the school because he paid taxes. Officer Binda [*3]  told [Appellant] that he would have 
to leave the school and he refused, demanding that he speak to a principal. [Appellant] stated that he "was not 
leaving until he spoke to a principal."

[Appellant] began to get very agitated. The vestibule at the high school is not secure and has direct access to the 
rest of the building. The main hallway where students were walking by was just 30 feet away. Officers viewed 
[Appellant] as a possible safety threat.

Officer Binda got up and began to escort [Appellant] out of the school, telling him multiple times that he would have 
to leave the premises. [Appellant] argued and refused to comply. It was clear that [Appellant] was not going to leave 
the building despite numerous directives to do so. At one point, [Appellant] stated that he would call the 
[Pennsylvania] State Police and the officers informed him that he would need to do that outside the building.

Officer Blinda then attempted to arrest [Appellant] for defiant trespassing when a scuffle ensued. Specifically, 
Officer Binda attempted to pull [Appellant] out the door while [Appellant] pushed back and attempted to remain 
inside. [Appellant] attempted to get back into the school and began wrestling [*4]  with

the two officers. Officer Binda and Chief Lander had to take [Appellant] to the ground outside the building. 
[Appellant] pushed the officers' hands away while scuffling with the officers. At one point, Chief Lander noted that 
[Appellant] "appeared to be bringing his fist back." [Appellant] was handcuffed and informed that he was under 
arrest at that time. Officer Binda suffered a laceration to his arm while wrestling with [Appellant].

On March 25, 2024, [after a non-jury trial,] the court entered a verdict finding [Appellant] "Guilty" of counts 3, 4, 5, 
and 6[,] and

"Not Guilty" of counts 1 and 2[.][3] [The court] stated its reasoning for the verdict [on the record]. This court 
sentenced [Appellant] on July 22, 2024, and placed him on one year of probation. [Appellant] filed timely post-
sentence motions on July 31, 2024. The Commonwealth filed a response to [the] post-sentence motion on August 
23, 2024. A hearing was scheduled for August 27, 2024. Just hours before the hearing, [Appellant] filed a 
supplemental post-sentence motion raising an additional claim.

Trial Court Opinion (TCO), 8/28/24, at 2-3 (unnumbered; citations omitted;



Page 3 of 13
Commonwealth v. Appellant, 2025 PA Super 244

emphasis in original; some capitalization altered). [*5] 

Appellant's post-sentence motion, including the issue raised in the

supplemental motion, was denied on August 28, 2024. He then filed a timely

notice of appeal on September 27, 2024. Pursuant to the trial court's order,

Appellant filed his concise statement of errors complained of on appeal on

October 21, 2024. In response, the trial court informed this Court that the

reasons for the denial of Appellant's issues on appeal could be found in the

opinion denying Appellant's post-sentence motions. Decree Pursuant to Rule

1925(a), 10/24/24. This appeal is now properly before this Court for

disposition.

3Count 1 charged Appellant with aggravated assault, 18 Pa.C.S. 2702(a)(3). Count 2 charged Appellant with simple 
assault, 18 Pa.C.S. 2701(a)(1).

Appellant puts forth seven issues on appeal, which we reorder for ease of disposition:

1. Whether the trial court erred by failing to address the lack of legal authority of the arresting officer to arrest 
Appellant for defiant trespass - an offense graded as at least a misdemeanor of the third degree - when the officer's 
authority was limited to summary offenses, thereby rendering the arrest, and consequently the resisting arrest 
charge, unlawful?

2. Whether the trial court erred in concluding that the [*6]  evidence was sufficient to sustain Appellant's conviction 
for defiant trespass under 18 Pa.C.S. 3503(b), where Appellant was wrongfully informed that his presence on 
school property was unlawful and [he] reasonably believed he was permitted to remain on the premises?

3. Whether the trial court erred in concluding that the evidence was sufficient to sustain Appellant's conviction for 
resisting arrest under 18 Pa.C.S. 5104, where the arrest was unlawful, Appellant reasonably believed that he was 
permitted to remain on school property to deliver paperwork, and the Commonwealth failed to prove that Appellant 
created a substantial risk of bodily injury or required substantial force to overcome his resistance?

4. Whether the trial court erred in concluding that the evidence was sufficient to sustain Appellant's conviction for 
disorderly conduct under 18 Pa.C.S. 5503(a)(1), where the Commonwealth failed to prove that Appellant engaged 
in fighting, threatening, or tumultuous behavior with [the] intent to cause public inconvenience, annoyance, or 
alarm?

5. Whether the trial court erred in concluding that the evidence was sufficient to sustain Appellant's conviction for 
harassment under 18 Pa.C.S. 2709(a)(1), where the Commonwealth failed to prove that Appellant acted [*7]  with 
the specific intent to harass, annoy, or alarm?

6. Whether the trial court erred in concluding that the verdicts of guilt for resisting arrest, defiant trespass, disorderly 
conduct, and harassment were not against the weight of the evidence, where Appellant's good-faith reliance on his 
medical exemption and the Secretary's Order undermined the Commonwealth's case?

7. Whether the trial court erred in denying Appellant's post-sentence motions for judgment of acquittal or, in the 
alternative, for a new trial, where the convictions were unsupported by sufficient evidence and against the weight of 
the evidence?



Page 4 of 13
Commonwealth v. Appellant, 2025 PA Super 244

Appellant's Brief at 3-5. We will address Appellant's claims seriatim.

Legal authority to arrest Appellant

Appellant first maintains that his arrest for defiant trespass was

unlawful. Specifically, Appellant argues, "[t]he arresting officer's lack of legal

authority to arrest Appellant for defiant trespass is a critical jurisdictional issue

that invalidates both the defiant trespass and resisting arrest charges."

Appellant's Brief at 20. Defiant trespass is a misdemeanor of the third degree

when the offender "defies an order to leave personally communicated to him

by the owner of the premises [*8]  or other authorized person." 18 Pa.C.S.

 3503(b)(2). Appellant argues that the school police were only authorized

to arrest persons for summary offenses and, since his offense was graded as

a misdemeanor, the arrest was unlawful.

We do not agree. Notably, the defiant trespass statute under

consideration can be deemed either a misdemeanor or a summary offense

under subsection (b)(2), as follows:

Except as provided in paragraph (1)(v), an offense under this subsection constitutes a misdemeanor of the third 
degree if the offender defies an order to leave personally communicated to him by the owner of the premises or 
other authorized person. An offense under paragraph (1)(v) constitutes a misdemeanor of the first degree. 
Otherwise it is a summary offense.

18 Pa.C.S. 3503(b)(2). Thus, by the plain language of the defiant trespass

statute, this crime could be graded as a misdemeanor of either the first or

third degree, or as a summary offense. Moreover, Pennsylvania law gives school police officers the authority to 
arrest for summary offenses. General duties of school police officers are enumerated in the Public School Code, as 
follows:

(a) General rule.--A school police officer appointed under section 1302-C(b) shall possess and exercise all the 
following powers and duties:

(1) To enforce good order in [*9]  school buildings, on school buses and on school grounds in the respective 
school entities….

***

(3) If authorized by the court, to issue summary citationsor to detain individuals who are in school buildings, 
on school buses and on school grounds in the respective school entities or nonpublic schools until local law 
enforcement is notified.

24 P.S. 13-1306-C(a)(1), (3) (emphasis added).



Page 5 of 13
Commonwealth v. Appellant, 2025 PA Super 244

Appellant argues that since he was charged with a misdemeanor, and school police only can arrest for summary 
charges, his arrest was improper. This argument misses the mark for two reasons. First, the officers clearly had 
probable cause to arrest Appellant for the lesser-graded offense of summary defiant trespass, even though he was 
ultimately charged and convicted of defiant trespass as a misdemeanor. Charging decisions in any case are made 
by prosecutors, not by police officers. See Commonwealth v. Cosby, 252

A.3d 1092, 1131 (Pa. 2021) ("As an 'administrator of justice,' the prosecutor has the power to decide whether to 
initiate formal criminal proceedings, to select those criminal charges which will be filed against the accused, to

negotiate plea bargains, to withdraw charges where appropriate, and, ultimately, to prosecute or dismiss [*10]  
charges at trial.") (emphasis added). Seealso Commonwealth v. Stipetich, 652 A.2d 1294, 1295 (Pa. 1995) 
(stating,

"[t]he district attorney's power to prosecute cannot be restricted by the actions of municipal police officers…. While 
the police exercise, as a practical matter, a certain discretion in deciding whether to make an arrest, … the ultimate 
discretion to file criminal charges lies in the district attorney.").

The prosecutor's decision to charge Appellant with a misdemeanor instead of a summary offense does not alter the 
conclusion that the police officer had probable cause to effectuate Appellant's arrest. Moreover, the school police 
were within their authority to detain someone on school grounds and wait for police to arrive. This was 
acknowledged by Officer Binda at trial. N.T. Trial, 3/25/24, at 8 ("We are … permitted to make summary arrests. 
Anything above a summary, we contact the state police."). Officer Binda noted that Appellant interacted with the 
school police for approximately 37 minutes on the day in question before the state police arrived. Id. at 14. Thus, 
the school police were within their authority to detain Appellant while waiting for the state police to arrive. In any 
event, the school police [*11]  officers did not exceed their authority under 24 P.S. 13-1306-C. Appellant was 
lawfully arrested.

Sufficiency claims

Appellant's next four issues allege that the evidence was insufficient to support each of his convictions. Because a 
determination of the sufficiency of

the evidence presents a question of law, "our standard of review is de novo

and our scope of review is plenary." Commonwealth v. Williams, 176 A.3d

298, 305 (Pa. Super. 2017). Further, we analyze this issue under the following

guidelines:

When reviewing challenges to the sufficiency of the evidence, we evaluate the record in the light most favorable to 
the Commonwealth as the verdict winner, giving the prosecution the benefit of all reasonable inferences to be 
drawn from the evidence. Evidence will be deemed sufficient to support the verdict when it establishes each 
material element of the crime charged and the commission thereof by the accused, beyond a reasonable doubt. 
However, the Commonwealth need not establish guilt to a mathematical certainty, and it may sustain its burden by 
means of wholly circumstantial evidence. Moreover, this Court may not substitute its judgment for that of the 
factfinder, and where the record contains support [*12]  for the convictions, they may not be disturbed. Lastly, we 
note that the finder of fact is free to believe some, all, or none of the evidence presented.

Commonwealth v. Toomer, 159 A.3d 956, 960-61 (Pa. Super. 2017) (internal citations and quotation marks 
omitted).

Commonwealth v. Ewida, 333 A.3d 1269, 1279 (Pa. Super. 2025).

Sufficiency of the evidence for defiant trespass



Page 6 of 13
Commonwealth v. Appellant, 2025 PA Super 244

Appellant contends that his conviction for defiant trespass is not

supported by sufficient evidence because the Commonwealth failed to prove

that he knowingly defied a lawful order to leave the premises. The statute

provides:

 3503. Criminal trespass

***

(b) Defiant trespasser.--

(1) A person commits an offense if, knowing that he is not licensed or privileged to do so, he enters or remains in 
any place as to which notice against trespass is given by:

(i) actual communication to the actor[.]

18 Pa.C.S. 3503(b)(1)(i). To establish this offense, "the Commonwealth must prove that a defendant (1) entered or 
remained upon property without a right to do; (2) while knowing that he had no license or privilege to be on the 
property; and (3) after receiving direct or indirect notice against trespass."

Commonwealth v. Powanda, 304 A.3d 1284, 1288 (Pa. Super. 2023).

Appellant claims that he had a "legitimate and lawful purpose of delivering paperwork related to changes in 
masking [*13]  policies[, and that he had] a good-faith belief that he was permitted to enter and remain." Appellant's

Brief at 14. Specifically, Appellant argues that it was unlawful to remove an individual from school grounds for failing 
to adhere to masking policies prevalent during the pandemic. Appellant states, without support from legal 
authorities, that he had a medical exemption from any masking requirement, making it unlawful to ask him to leave 
the school building.

Appellant's argument entirely misses the point. He was not removed from the school building because he refused to 
wear a mask; he was removed from the building because he did not have an appointment with any school 
personnel and thus had no legitimate reason to be on the premises. This case is analogous to Commonwealth v. 
Downing, 511 A.2d 792 (Pa. 1986). There, the appellant, not a student of Temple University or its law school, 
obtained a library card in order to access the law school's library during its

normal hours of operation. Id. at 793. In December of 1980, access to the library was restricted to law students 
studying for final exams. Id. Downing asked the school's administration for access to the library during this time, but 
his request was denied. [*14]  Id. Downing then left the building, but returned about a week later, again asking to be 
admitted into the library "because it was his right." Id. When Downing refused to leave, campus police placed him 
under arrest for defiant trespass and disorderly conduct.

On appeal, Downing argued that the library was open to members of the public at the time he attempted to enter, 
which is a defense to the defiant trespass charge. However, our Supreme Court held that the law library was only 
open to non-students if they asked for and obtained a library pass, which was revokable at the law school's 
pleasure. Id. at 795. Downing's permission to be at the library was revoked during exam time. Thus, the defense did 
not apply. Id. Importantly, "[o]nce permission to enter and use the facility is revoked, the privilege or license to use 
the library ceases." Id. Since the law school chose to terminate his privilege to use the library during law school 
exams, and Downing was fully aware that his license to use the library had been revoked, the conviction for defiant 
trespass was affirmed. Id.

The same result applies here. Appellant may have thought that he had a right to be on the property, but once he 
was told [*15]  that he could not remain in the building without an appointment, any right to remain clearly ceased. 



Page 7 of 13
Commonwealth v. Appellant, 2025 PA Super 244

Appellant was repeatedly told that he could not remain on the site without an appointment, yet he refused to comply 
with the school police officers' orders

to leave. The evidence is sufficient to support his conviction for defiant

trespass. Id. See also Commonwealth v. Conyers, 357 A.2d 569, 570

(Pa. Super. 1976) (en banc) ("The crime of defiant trespass occurs when a

person remains in a place where he is not privileged to remain after notice of

trespass is given.").

Sufficiency of the evidence for resisting arrest

Appellant next challenges his conviction for resisting arrest. The Crimes

Code provides:

 5104. Resisting arrest or other law enforcement

A person commits a misdemeanor of the second degree if, with the intent of preventing a public servant from 
effecting a lawful arrest or discharging any other duty, the person creates a substantial risk of bodily injury to the 
public servant or anyone else, or employs means justifying or requiring substantial force to overcome the 
resistance.

18 Pa.C.S. 5104. This offense requires proof that a public servant was

affecting a lawful arrest or discharging a legal duty other than an arrest, [*16]  which

the defendant intended to prevent. See Commonwealth v. Karl, 476 A.2d

908, 911 (Pa. Super. 1984). The Commonwealth does not need to establish

actual injury. Commonwealth v. Lyons, 555 A.2d 920, 925 (Pa. Super.

1989). Rather, to support a conviction for resisting arrest, the Commonwealth

may prove either that the defendant's actions created a substantial risk of

serious bodily injury or that the defendant employed means justifying or

requiring substantial force to overcome the resistance. Id.

Herein, Appellant initially argues that the evidence was insufficient

under Commonwealth v. Biagini, 655 A.2d 492 (Pa. 1995), because "in order to be convicted of resisting arrest, 
the underlying arrest must be lawful."

Id. at 497. As noted in his first issue, Appellant maintains that his arrest was unlawful because school authorities 
are only provided with the authority to arrest for summary offenses, while he was charged with a misdemeanor of 
the third-degree. However, we determined above that the school police officers were within their power to arrest 
Appellant. Accordingly, Biagini does not require that the resisting arrest conviction be overturned.

Appellant also argues that the evidence was insufficient because the Commonwealth failed to establish [*17]  that 
his actions either created a substantial risk of bodily injury4 or required substantial force to overcome his resistance. 
In essence, Appellant contends that this was a minor scuffle and that he posed no danger to anyone. Yet, whether 



Page 8 of 13
Commonwealth v. Appellant, 2025 PA Super 244

Appellant actually inflicted a bodily injury to the officers is irrelevant. "Merely exposing another to the risk of such 
injury is sufficient to sustain a conviction under Section 5104." Commonwealth v.Taylor-Dixon, 322 A.3d 966, 970 
(Pa. Super. 2024). Here, Appellant entered the school building and wanted to speak to a principal. N.T. Trial at 8. 
Officer Binda asked if Appellant had an appointment, and Appellant stated that he did not. Id. at 9. Since Appellant 
had a folder of information that he wanted the principal to have, Officer Binda offered to take it to the principal, but 
Appellant refused that suggestion. Id. Instead, Appellant told the officer that he had

4 Our Crimes Code defines "bodily injury" in this context as the "[i]mpairment of physical condition or substantial 
pain." 18 Pa.C.S. 2301.

spoken to an attorney, knew he had a right to be on the property because he pays taxes, and refused to exit the 
building. Id. Officer Binda told Appellant multiple times that he could not be inside the building [*18]  without an 
appointment, but he refused to leave. Id. at 10. Officer Binda and Chief Lander then physically escorted Appellant 
out of the school building, with Appellant wrestling with the officers in an attempt to re-enter. Id. at 10-11. During 
this 'scuffle', the officers and Appellant all fell onto the pavement outside the school doors. Id. at 11. Appellant 
flailed his arms to prevent the officers from handcuffing him. Id. at 13-14. Officer Binda was injured during this 
incident, sustaining a laceration to his forearm. Id.

This evidence is clearly sufficient to support Appellant's conviction for resisting arrest. Appellant's belief that he 
could not be ejected from the school due to his failing to wear a mask does not alter the fact that he was repeatedly 
told that he was not permitted to be inside the building without an appointment. Critically, however, the officers had 
to physically wrestle with Appellant to eject him from the building. During the quest to move Appellant outside, the 
officers had to grapple with Appellant. Appellant's acts caused the parties to fall to the pavement before officers 
could place him in handcuffs, during which an officer sustained a cut to his forearm. [*19]  These acts show that 
Appellant at least exposed the officers to the risk of bodily injury, if not caused it, and that they had to utilize 
substantial force to restrain him. Viewing the evidence in the light most favorable to the Commonwealth, as we must 
do under our standard of review, we find the evidence sufficient to support

Appellant's resisting arrest conviction. See Taylor-Dixon, supra (affirming a conviction for resisting arrest where 
the defendant pulled away from the officer's touch on his arm and began to run, then, when subdued, he refused to 
put his hands behind his back, elbowed the officer in the eye and attempted to grab the officer's taser; such acts 
meant the officers had to use substantial force to overcome his resistance); Commonwealth v. Becker, No. 710 
MDA 2024, 2025 WL 1625549 (Pa. Super. June 9, 2025) (unpublished memorandum) (finding sufficient evidence 
for resisting arrest where the defendant refused to enter the police car after being handcuffed, he "tensed up" and 
"put up a pretty good struggle," including kicking an officer in the head hard enough to make the officer dizzy).5

Sufficiency of the evidence for disorderly conduct

Appellant's next claim alleges that the evidence was insufficient to support his conviction for [*20]  disorderly 
conduct because the Commonwealth failed to prove that he engaged in fighting, threatening, or tumultuous 
behavior with the intent to cause public inconvenience, annoyance, or alarm. The disorderly conduct statute 
provides, in pertinent part:

5503. Disorderly conduct

(a) Offense Defined.--A person is guilty of disorderly conduct if, with intent to cause public inconvenience, 
annoyance or alarm, or recklessly creating a risk thereof, he:



Page 9 of 13
Commonwealth v. Appellant, 2025 PA Super 244

5Non-precedential memorandum decisions from the Superior Court filed after May 1, 2019, may be cited for their 
persuasive value under Pa.R.A.P. 126(b).

(1) engages in fighting or threatening, or in violent or tumultuous behavior[.]

18 Pa.C.S. 5503(a)(1). The purpose behind Section 5503 is to protect the public from public unruliness leading to 
tumult or disorder; it is not a "catchall for every act which annoys or disturbs people." Commonwealth v. Coniker, 
290 A.3d 725, 735 (Pa. Super. 2023). Rather, Section 5503 requires proof that the defendant either intended to 
cause public inconvenience, annoyance or alarm, or recklessly created a risk of causing such. Id. Therefore, the 
Commonwealth can "sustain a disorderly conduct conviction with evidence that the defendant recklessly created a 
risk of public inconvenience, annoyance, or alarm, even [*21]  if he lacked the intent to do so." Id. "The cardinal 
feature of the crime of disorderly conduct is public unruliness which can or does lead to tumult and disorder." 
Commonwealth v. Hock, 728 A.2d 943, 946 (Pa. 1999).

Appellant cites Hock as support for his contention that a disorderly conduct conviction is not established by conduct 
that merely annoys others. In Hock, the defendant, whom authorities knew had no valid driver's license, was seen 
driving into her apartment complex. Id. at 944. A police officer followed Hock's car into the lot and, as she exited her 
car, asked to see her license. Id. The officer responded to Hock's refusal to comply by stating that she would 
receive a citation in the mail. Id. Hock walked away from the area, saying, in a normal tone of voice, "F*** you, 
A******." Id. No person other than Hock and the officer were present. On appeal, our Supreme Court reversed 
Hock's disorderly conduct conviction, stating that the offense of

disorderly conduct has a specific purpose - "it is intended to preserve the public peace[,]" that Hock's epithet was 
not an example of "fighting words" in that the comment did not frighten or alarm the officer, and the fact that no 
bystanders were present precluded Hock's [*22]  conviction.

Appellant claims that his presence on school grounds was for a lawful purpose - to deliver his "paperwork" about 
masking policies - and he never intended to case public inconvenience, annoyance, or alarm. Yet, Appellant did not 
attend that school, and none of Appellant's children attended the school in question. The school building was 
currently in operation and full of students; indeed, a student was present in the lobby when this incident occurred. 
Appellant blames the officers for the incident.

After review, we conclude that the evidence at trial evinces that, at a minimum, Appellant acted recklessly and 
created a risk of public inconvenience, annoyance, or alarm by his actions. While Appellant may not have intended 
to create a disturbance by his unannounced appearance at the school, his refusal to exit after being told to do so, 
and his physical interaction with the officers after being told that he had to leave the building, created a hazardous 
and/or alarming condition for the parties involved. Accordingly, disorderly conduct was proven in this case. See 
Coniker, supra (upholding a conviction for disorderly conduct where the defendant made statements about having 
non-violent [*23]  weapons in a courtroom and a lawyer's office, despite the defendant's lack of specific intent to 
annoy or alarm; such a statement created a hazardous condition that involved danger or a risk of

injury to surrounding citizens and served no legitimate purpose);

Commonwealth v. McConnell, 244 A.3d 44 (Pa. Super. 2020) (affirming disorderly conduct conviction for a 
defendant who installed eight high-powered construction floodlights to illuminate his neighbor's back yard in an 
attempt to protest the neighbor's backyard pool lighting, his "protest" was unreasonable and offensive and served 
no legitimate purpose). In sum,

Appellant's act of refusing to exit the school building and physically engaging with the police as they tried to get him 
to leave, when he had no legitimate reason to be on the property, amounts to tumultuous behavior which he should 
have known would cause public disturbance or alarm. The evidence is sufficient to support Appellant's disorderly 
conduct conviction.

Sufficiency of the evidence for harassment



Page 10 of 13
Commonwealth v. Appellant, 2025 PA Super 244

Appellant also challenges his conviction for harassment. The statute provides:

2709. Harassment

(a) Offense defined.-A person commits the crime of harassment when, with intent to harass, annoy or alarm 
another, [*24]  the person:

(1) strikes, shoves, kicks or otherwise subjects the other person to physical contact, or attempts or threatens to do 
the same[.]

18 Pa.C.S. 2709(a)(1). The intent to harass may be inferred from the

totality of the circumstances. Commonwealth v. Miyares, 320 A.3d 740,

743 (Pa. Super. 2024).

Appellant maintains on appeal that he did not have the specific intent to

harass, annoy, or alarm anyone as required by the statute. Specifically, he

argues:

Appellant's actions were defensive and limited to responding to the officers' conduct. There is no evidence in the 
record that

Appellant acted with any intent to harass, annoy, or alarm the officers or anyone else. His presence on school 
property was for a lawful and legitimate purpose - delivering paperwork related to masking policies - and his 
conduct did not exceed the bounds of reasonable resistance to an unwarranted and unlawful removal. Without 
proof of specific intent, the Commonwealth has failed to meet its burden, and the harassment conviction cannot 
stand.

Appellant's Brief at 19.

Appellant fails to adhere to our standard of review in that he does not

address the facts in the light most favorable to the Commonwealth as the

verdict winner. Officer Binda testified at [*25]  Appellant's trial about the

circumstances of his removal from the school entryway:

[Officer Binda]: At that time I started to escort [Appellant] outside, got him to the door, get him outside. I told him 
he'd have to leave the premises. He still wanted to argue with us and not leave. At that time I went to place him 
under arrest for defiant trespassing, and then that's when the scuffle ensued, and we had to take [Appellant] to the 
ground.

***

He tried to get back into the school. We grabbed him. Me and him started to tussle. Started wrestling on our feet. At 
one point my chief had to grab ahold of him because he said he believed that he was going to try to swing at me. 
When we did, we went down to the ground.

Case Name: Commonwealth v. Bettis, 2025 PA Super 244.
Court: Superior Court of Pennsylvania.
Area of Law: Criminal Law—Arrest Authority; Sufficiency of Evidence.
Procedural Posture: Appeal from a judgment of sentence following a non-jury trial conviction.
Issue
The appellant appeals his judgment of sentence for defiant trespass, resisting arrest, disorderly conduct, and harassment stemming from an incident where he refused to leave a high school after being denied entry for lacking an appointment. The central legal inquiry is whether school police officers possess the statutory authority to effectuate an arrest for defiant trespass when the offense is graded as a misdemeanor rather than a summary offense, and whether the officers' authority to detain individuals pending local law enforcement arrival validates the arrest. Furthermore, the court must determine if the evidence was sufficient to establish the requisite mens rea and actus reus for the convictions, particularly given the appellant's subjective belief that he had a right to be on the premises to protest school policies and his contention that his physical resistance was merely defensive.
Rule
Under the Public School Code, school police officers are authorized to enforce good order and issue summary citations or detain individuals until local law enforcement arrives (24 P.S. § 13-1306-C). Defiant trespass occurs when a person remains in a place knowing they lack privilege to do so after receiving notice to leave (18 Pa.C.S. § 3503). Resisting arrest requires creating a substantial risk of bodily injury or requiring substantial force to overcome resistance to a lawful arrest (18 Pa.C.S. § 5104). Disorderly conduct involves creating a hazardous or physically offensive condition by an act that serves no legitimate purpose (18 Pa.C.S. § 5503). Harassment requires an intent to harass, annoy, or alarm another through physical contact (18 Pa.C.S. § 2709).
Application
The court rejected the appellant's argument that his arrest was unlawful because school police are limited to summary arrests. The court held that the officers had probable cause for the summary offense of defiant trespass, and the prosecutor's subsequent decision to charge a misdemeanor did not invalidate the initial arrest [*10]. Furthermore, the statute explicitly authorizes school police to detain individuals until local police arrive.
Regarding sufficiency, the court found the evidence supported the defiant trespass conviction because the appellant's license to be on school property was revoked when he was told he could not remain without an appointment; his belief regarding mask exemptions was irrelevant to the lack of an appointment [*15]. For resisting arrest, the court found that the "scuffle" requiring two officers to wrestle the appellant to the ground, resulting in an officer's laceration, constituted substantial force and risk of injury [*18]. The disorderly conduct conviction was upheld because the appellant's refusal to leave a school full of students created a hazardous condition and risk of public alarm [*22]. Finally, the harassment conviction was supported by testimony that the appellant became combative, flailed his arms, and appeared to prepare to punch an officer, allowing an inference of intent to harass or alarm [*26].
Conclusion
The judgment of sentence is affirmed.

Opinion

 [*1] FOR PLAINTIFF-APPELLEE: PENN A. DODSON,

AndersonDodson, P.C., New

York, NY
